rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.subtopic: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation and the Photon
rows.stem: The momentum of a photon associated with a microwave of wavelength \(4{\cdot}00\) cm is :
rows.solution:
**The answer is (A): \(1{\cdot}66\times 10^{-32}\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).**

**A photon's momentum depends only on its wavelength:**

\(p = \dfrac{h}{\lambda}\)

**Convert the wavelength to metres first** — this is where the question is won or lost:

\(\lambda = 4{\cdot}00\ \mathrm{cm} = 4{\cdot}00\times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m}\)

**Substituting:**

\(p = \dfrac{6{\cdot}63\times 10^{-34}}{4{\cdot}00\times 10^{-2}} = 1{\cdot}66\times 10^{-32}\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\)

\(\boxed{\ p = 1{\cdot}66\times 10^{-32}\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\ }\)

**Option (D) carries the same mantissa with the wrong exponent**, and it is exactly what appears if the centimetre is ignored and \(\lambda\) taken as \(4\) metres: \(6{\cdot}63\times 10^{-34}/4 = 1{\cdot}66\times 10^{-34}\). **Two options differing only by \(10^{2}\) is the signature of a unit trap**, and it is worth treating any such pair as a warning to re-check the conversion.

**Why \(p = h/\lambda\) and not \(mv\).** A photon has no rest mass, so \(mv\) is meaningless for it. Its momentum follows from the relativistic relation for a massless particle:

\(E = pc \qquad\text{and}\qquad E = h\nu \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad p = \dfrac{h\nu}{c} = \dfrac{h}{\lambda}\)

**The same expression that de Broglie later applied to matter** — which is the point of the pairing: \(p = h/\lambda\) holds for photons and electrons alike, and it is the one relation the two pictures share.

**How small is this momentum?** Compare an electron moving at a mere \(1\) m/s: \(p = 9{\cdot}1\times 10^{-31}\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\), some **fifty times larger**. A microwave photon carries extraordinarily little momentum, which is why radiation pressure is negligible in everyday circumstances and measurable only with intense beams or over astronomical distances — as in a comet's tail, or a solar sail.

**The corresponding energy**, for scale:

\(E = pc = \left(1{\cdot}66\times 10^{-32}\right)\left(3\times 10^{8}\right) = 4{\cdot}97\times 10^{-24}\ \mathrm{J} = 3{\cdot}1\times 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV}\)

**About thirty microelectronvolts** — far too little to break any chemical bond, which is why microwaves heat by making molecules rotate rather than by ionising them.

rows.stem: Two point charges \(-\mathrm{Q}\) and \(\mathrm{Q}\) are located at points (d, 0) and (0, d) respectively, in x-y plane. The electric field \(\vec{\mathrm{E}}\) at the origin will be :
rows.solution:
**The answer is (C): \(\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{Q}{d^{2}}\left(\hat{i} - \hat{j}\right)\).**

**Both charges are the same distance \(d\) from the origin**, so both produce a field of the same magnitude there:

\(E_1 = E_2 = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\dfrac{Q}{d^{2}}\)

**The whole question is the two DIRECTIONS**, and each is settled by the sign of its charge.

**The \(-Q\) at \(\left(d, 0\right)\).** A field points **towards** a negative charge, so at the origin it points from the origin **towards** \(\left(d, 0\right)\) — that is, along \(+\hat{i}\):

\(\vec{E}_1 = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\dfrac{Q}{d^{2}}\,\hat{i}\)

**The \(+Q\) at \(\left(0, d\right)\).** A field points **away** from a positive charge, so at the origin it points from \(\left(0, d\right)\) towards the origin and onward — that is, along \(-\hat{j}\):

\(\vec{E}_2 = -\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\dfrac{Q}{d^{2}}\,\hat{j}\)

**Adding**, since the two are perpendicular and simply combine as components:

\(\boxed{\ \vec{E} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\dfrac{Q}{d^{2}}\left(\hat{i} - \hat{j}\right)\ }\)

**The \(\sqrt{2}\) in options (A) and (B) is the significant trap.** It is the **magnitude** of the resultant, since the two perpendicular components of equal size give

\(\left|\vec{E}\right| = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt{2}\,Q}{d^{2}}\)

**But \(\left(\hat{i} - \hat{j}\right)\) is NOT a unit vector** — its own magnitude is \(\sqrt{2}\). Writing \(\sqrt{2}\,Q/d^{2}\) **and** the bracket applies the factor twice and doubles the field. The correct forms are either \(\left(Q/d^{2}\right)\left(\hat{i}-\hat{j}\right)\) or \(\left(\sqrt{2}Q/d^{2}\right)\left(\hat{i}-\hat{j}\right)/\sqrt{2}\), never both.

**Option (D) has both signs wrong**, which corresponds to swapping the two charges — \(+Q\) on the \(x\)-axis and \(-Q\) on the \(y\)-axis. Reading which charge sits where is half of this question.

**The resultant points into the FOURTH quadrant**, at \(-45^\circ\) to the \(x\)-axis — bisecting the directions of the two contributions, as equal perpendicular components must.

**A physical reading.** The pair \(-Q\) and \(+Q\) is a dipole whose moment points from the negative to the positive charge, that is from \(\left(d,0\right)\) towards \(\left(0,d\right)\), along \(\left(-\hat{i} + \hat{j}\right)\). **The field at the origin is antiparallel to that**, which is exactly what is expected on the perpendicular bisector — the origin lies on the equatorial line of this dipole, where the field opposes \(\vec{p}\).

rows.stem: An electron is moving with velocity \(v_0\,\hat{i}\). If a uniform electric field \(\vec{\mathrm{E}} = \mathrm{E}_0\,\hat{j}\) is set up in the region, the electron will :
rows.solution:
**The answer is (C): describe a parabolic path.**

**Set out the two vectors.** The electron's initial velocity is along \(+x\); the electric field is along \(+y\). The force on it is

\(\vec{F} = q\vec{E} = \left(-e\right)E_0\,\hat{j} = -eE_0\,\hat{j}\)

**so the force is along \(-\hat{j}\)** — opposite to the field, because the electron's charge is negative.

**The force is CONSTANT in magnitude and direction, and PERPENDICULAR to the initial velocity.** That combination is the whole answer, and it is exactly the situation of a projectile under gravity.

**Resolving the motion:**

\(\text{along } x: \quad a_x = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x = v_0t\)

\(\text{along } y: \quad a_y = -\dfrac{eE_0}{m} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad y = -\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{eE_0}{m}t^{2}\)

**Eliminating \(t\)** using \(t = x/v_0\):

\(y = -\dfrac{eE_0}{2mv_0^{2}}\,x^{2}\)

\(\boxed{\ y \propto -x^{2}\ \text{— a PARABOLA opening downwards}\ }\)

**Option (A), a circle, requires a force of constant MAGNITUDE that always stays perpendicular to the velocity** — it must turn as the particle turns. An electric field does not: it keeps pointing along \(+\hat{j}\) whatever the electron does, so the angle between force and velocity changes continuously. **That is the essential difference between an electric and a magnetic force**, and it is why a magnetic field gives circles while an electric field gives parabolas.

**Option (B), a helix, arises in a MAGNETIC field when the velocity has a component along \(\vec{B}\)** — circular motion perpendicular to the field combined with uniform drift along it. It needs a magnetic force, which is absent here.

**Option (D) would require zero net force**, but \(\vec{E}\) is perpendicular to \(\vec{v}\), not parallel, so it certainly deflects the electron. *(Had \(\vec{E}\) been along \(\hat{i}\), the electron would have moved in a straight line — decelerating, then reversing, but never deviating.)*

**The speed is NOT constant**, unlike the magnetic case. The force has a component along the velocity as soon as the path begins to bend, so the electric field does work and the electron **gains** kinetic energy:

\(\dfrac{1}{2}mv^{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}mv_0^{2} + eE_0\left|y\right|\)

**A magnetic force never does work; an electric force generally does.** That is the second half of the same distinction.

**This is the deflecting mechanism of a cathode-ray tube** — an electron beam fired past charged plates follows precisely this parabola inside the plates, then travels in a straight line to the screen.

rows.subtopic: Magnetic Force and Motion in a Magnetic Field
rows.stem: A charged particle of mass m having kinetic energy K passes undeflected through a region with electric field \(\vec{\mathrm{E}}\) and magnetic field \(\vec{\mathrm{B}}\) acting perpendicular to each other. The mass m of the particle will be :
rows.solution:
**The answer is (B): \(\dfrac{2KB^{2}}{E^{2}}\).**

**"Passes undeflected" through crossed fields means the electric and magnetic forces CANCEL.** That is the velocity-selector condition, and it fixes the speed.

\(qE = qvB\)

**The charge cancels — which is the striking feature of the arrangement:**

\(\boxed{\ v = \dfrac{E}{B}\ }\)

**Only particles of this one speed pass undeflected**, whatever their charge or mass. That is what makes the device a **selector**: a beam of mixed speeds enters and a single speed emerges.

**Now bring in the kinetic energy.**

\(K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^{2} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad m = \dfrac{2K}{v^{2}}\)

**Substituting \(v = E/B\):**

\(m = \dfrac{2K}{\left(E/B\right)^{2}} = \dfrac{2KB^{2}}{E^{2}}\)

\(\boxed{\ m = \dfrac{2KB^{2}}{E^{2}}\ }\)

**Options (C) and (D) have \(E\) and \(B\) the wrong way round.** A dimensional check settles it without any physics: \(E/B\) has the dimensions of a velocity, so \(K/v^{2}\) requires \(B^{2}/E^{2}\) in the numerator. **\(KE^{2}/B^{2}\) would be \(K\) multiplied by a squared velocity — an energy times a velocity squared, which is not a mass.**

**Option (A) has the factor of \(2\) inverted**, from writing \(K = 2mv^{2}\) or \(m = K/2v^{2}\). The \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) in the kinetic energy becomes a \(2\) when \(m\) is made the subject.

**Note the charge \(q\) never appears in the answer**, and that is not an accident. It cancelled at the first step and never returned, so **the same crossed fields select the same speed for a proton, an electron or an alpha particle**. The mass then follows from the kinetic energy alone.

**The geometry the phrase implies.** \(\vec{E}\), \(\vec{B}\) and \(\vec{v}\) must be **mutually perpendicular** for the two forces to be antiparallel and capable of cancelling. If \(\vec{v}\) were along \(\vec{B}\) the magnetic force would vanish entirely and nothing could balance \(qE\).

**Where this is used.** It is the front end of a **mass spectrometer** (Thomson's and Bainbridge's): the selector delivers a beam of known speed, which is then bent by a second magnetic field into a circle of radius \(r = mv/qB'\). Measuring \(r\) gives \(m/q\) directly — the experiment that first established the existence of isotopes.

rows.stem: A rectangular loop of size 5 cm \(\times\) 8 cm is lying in x-y plane in a uniform magnetic field \(\vec{\mathrm{B}} = (2{\cdot}0\ \mathrm{T})\ \hat{k}\). The total magnetic flux linked with the loop is :
rows.solution:
**The answer is (D): \(8\times 10^{-3}\) Wb.**

**The loop lies in the \(xy\)-plane, so its area vector is along \(\hat{k}\)** — exactly parallel to the field. The flux is therefore simply \(BA\), with no \(\cos\theta\) to worry about:

\(\Phi = \vec{B}\cdot\vec{A} = BA\cos 0^\circ = BA\)

**The area, converted to SI:**

\(A = 5\ \mathrm{cm}\times 8\ \mathrm{cm} = 40\ \mathrm{cm^{2}}\)

\(1\ \mathrm{cm^{2}} = \left(10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m}\right)^{2} = 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^{2}}\)

\(A = 40\times 10^{-4} = 4\times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^{2}}\)

**The flux:**

\(\Phi = \left(2{\cdot}0\right)\left(4\times 10^{-3}\right)\)

\(\boxed{\ \Phi = 8\times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{Wb}\ }\)

**The conversion \(\mathrm{cm^{2}} \to \mathrm{m^{2}}\) is \(10^{-4}\), not \(10^{-2}\)** — a centimetre **each way**. Option (A), \(80\) Wb, is the answer with no conversion at all \(\left(2{\cdot}0\times 40\right)\), and option (C) is the right figure with the exponent one place out. **Three of the four options are the same calculation with different powers of ten**, which is the clearest possible signal that the units are the whole question.

**A sense of scale.** \(8\) milliwebers is a small flux, and \(2\) T is a strong field — comparable to a clinical MRI magnet. Option (A)'s \(80\) Wb would be an extraordinary quantity, the sort of number that should prompt a re-check on sight.

**Why the orientation was given, and what it saves.** Had the loop been tilted at \(\theta\) to the field, the flux would be \(BA\cos\theta\) and an extra factor would be needed. Lying in the \(xy\)-plane with \(\vec{B}\) along \(\hat{k}\) puts \(\vec{B}\) **perpendicular to the loop's plane** and **parallel to its normal** — the configuration of maximum flux.

**A caution about "perpendicular".** A field perpendicular to the **plane** is parallel to the **area vector**, and gives \(\cos 0 = 1\). A field lying **in** the plane is perpendicular to the area vector and gives zero flux. The two phrasings describe opposite situations, and reading which one is meant is a recurring hazard in flux problems.

**No emf is induced here.** The field is uniform and steady and the loop is stationary, so \(d\Phi/dt = 0\). Flux and induced emf are different quantities: a large steady flux produces nothing at all.

rows.subtopic: Bohr Model of the Hydrogen Atom
rows.stem: The energy of an electron revolving in the \(n^{th}\) orbit in Bohr model of hydrogen atom is proportional to :
rows.solution:
**The answer is (D): \(\dfrac{1}{n^{2}}\).**

**The Bohr energy levels of hydrogen:**

\(E_n = -\dfrac{13{\cdot}6}{n^{2}}\ \mathrm{eV} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \boxed{\ E_n \propto \dfrac{1}{n^{2}}\ }\)

**Where the \(1/n^{2}\) comes from.** Two results combine. The total energy of the orbiting electron is

\(E = -\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\dfrac{e^{2}}{2r}\)

so \(E \propto -1/r\); and the Bohr radii grow as \(r_n = n^{2}a_0\). Substituting gives \(E_n \propto -1/n^{2}\).

**Option (A), \(n^{2}\), is the RADIUS's dependence** — the most quoted Bohr result, and the natural slip. The energy varies as its **reciprocal**, because a larger orbit means a more weakly bound electron.

**The sign matters and the question's phrasing glosses it.** All the \(E_n\) are **negative**, since the electron is bound; the zero of energy is taken at infinite separation. So the energies **rise towards zero** as \(n\) increases, while their **magnitudes** fall as \(1/n^{2}\). Strictly, \(E_n\) is proportional to \(1/n^{2}\) with a negative constant of proportionality.

**In figures:**

\(E_1 = -13{\cdot}6, \quad E_2 = -3{\cdot}40, \quad E_3 = -1{\cdot}51, \quad E_4 = -0{\cdot}85\ \mathrm{eV}\)

**The levels CROWD TOGETHER as \(n\) grows**, and that is the visible consequence of the \(1/n^{2}\) law. The gap from \(n=1\) to \(2\) is \(10{\cdot}2\) eV; from \(2\) to \(3\) only \(1{\cdot}89\) eV; from \(3\) to \(4\) just \(0{\cdot}66\) eV. **The whole infinite ladder above the ground state is contained within \(13{\cdot}6\) eV**, which is why every spectral series converges to a limit rather than running on indefinitely.

**The companion dependences**, worth holding together, since options (B) and (C) are each a genuine Bohr result attached to the wrong quantity:

\(r_n \propto n^{2}, \qquad v_n \propto \dfrac{1}{n}, \qquad L_n \propto n, \qquad T_n \propto n^{3}, \qquad E_n \propto -\dfrac{1}{n^{2}}\)

**For a hydrogen-like ion of nuclear charge \(Z\)** the law generalises to \(E_n = -13{\cdot}6\,Z^{2}/n^{2}\) eV, so \(\mathrm{He^{+}}\) is bound four times as tightly as hydrogen in every level.

rows.stem: In a Young's double-slit experiment, two waves each of intensity I superpose each other and produce an interference pattern. Prove that the resultant intensities at maxima and minima are 4 I and zero respectively.
rows.solution:
**Two coherent waves of equal intensity \(I\) superpose.** Since intensity goes as the square of amplitude, write \(I = ka^{2}\), so each wave has amplitude \(a\).

**The resultant amplitude** for two waves of amplitude \(a\) with phase difference \(\phi\):

\(A^{2} = a^{2} + a^{2} + 2a^{2}\cos\phi = 2a^{2}\left(1 + \cos\phi\right)\)

**and the resultant intensity:**

\(I_R = I_1 + I_2 + 2\sqrt{I_1I_2}\cos\phi = 2I + 2I\cos\phi\)

**AT A MAXIMUM.** The waves arrive **in phase**, \(\phi = 0\) and \(\cos\phi = +1\):

\(I_{\max} = 2I + 2I = 4I\)

\(\boxed{\ I_{\max} = 4I\ }\)

*Equivalently, through amplitudes:* \(I_{\max} = \left(\sqrt{I_1} + \sqrt{I_2}\right)^{2} = \left(2\sqrt{I}\right)^{2} = 4I\) \(\checkmark\)

**AT A MINIMUM.** The waves arrive **exactly out of phase**, \(\phi = \pi\) and \(\cos\phi = -1\):

\(I_{\min} = 2I - 2I = 0\)

\(\boxed{\ I_{\min} = 0\ }\)

*Equivalently:* \(I_{\min} = \left(\sqrt{I_1} - \sqrt{I_2}\right)^{2} = 0\), since the two intensities are equal. **Complete darkness requires exactly equal amplitudes**, and it is the only case in which the minima are truly black.

**\(4I\), NOT \(2I\), is the point of the question.** Two beams each of intensity \(I\) might be expected to give \(2I\) where they reinforce. They give **four times** one beam, because it is the **amplitudes** that add, not the intensities, and \(\left(a + a\right)^{2} = 4a^{2}\).

**No energy is created.** The surplus at the maxima is exactly balanced by the deficit at the minima. Averaging \(I_R = 2I\left(1 + \cos\phi\right)\) over a full cycle of \(\phi\) gives

\(\left\langle I_R\right\rangle = 2I\)

**— precisely the \(2I\) that arrives.** Interference **redistributes** energy across the screen; it never adds or destroys any. That is the answer to the standard objection that a dark fringe seems to make light vanish.

**The general intensity distribution**, which contains both results:

\(I_R = 4I\cos^{2}\left(\dfrac{\phi}{2}\right)\)

*Setting \(\phi = 0\) gives \(4I\); setting \(\phi = \pi\) gives zero.* **Note the HALF-angle** — the argument is \(\phi/2\), not \(\phi\), and that is where this formula is usually misapplied.

**Why the sources must be coherent.** If \(\phi\) varied randomly in time, \(\cos\phi\) would average to zero and \(I_R\) would be a uniform \(2I\) everywhere — no pattern at all. **A steady phase relationship is what allows the \(\cos\phi\) term to survive**, and it is why the two slits must be fed from one source.

rows.stem: A square loop of side 10 cm, free to rotate about a vertical axis coinciding with its one arm, is initially held perpendicular to a uniform horizontal magnetic field of \(0{\cdot}2\) T. If it is rotated at the uniform speed of 60 rpm, find the emf induced in the loop.
rows.solution:
**A loop rotating in a magnetic field is an AC GENERATOR**, and the emf it produces is

\(\varepsilon = NBA\omega\sin\omega t\)

**with peak value** \(\varepsilon_0 = NBA\omega\).

**Gather the quantities.**

\(A = \left(10\ \mathrm{cm}\right)^{2} = \left(0{\cdot}1\ \mathrm{m}\right)^{2} = 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m^{2}} = 100\times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^{2}}\)

\(B = 0{\cdot}2\ \mathrm{T}, \qquad N = 1\ \left(\text{a single loop}\right)\)

**The angular speed — convert from rpm:**

\(60\ \text{rpm} = \dfrac{60}{60} = 1\ \text{revolution per second} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \omega = 2\pi\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\)

**Substituting:**

\(\varepsilon_0 = \left(0{\cdot}2\right)\left(10^{-2}\right)\left(2\pi\right) = 4\pi\times 10^{-3}\)

\(\boxed{\ \varepsilon_0 = 12{\cdot}56\times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{V} \approx 12{\cdot}6\ \mathrm{mV}\ }\)

**and the instantaneous emf is** \(\varepsilon = 12{\cdot}56\times 10^{-3}\sin 2\pi t\ \mathrm{V}\).

**Converting rpm to \(\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\) is the step that carries the risk.** Sixty revolutions per **minute** is one per second, and each revolution is \(2\pi\) radians — so \(\omega = 2\pi\), not \(60\). Using \(60\) directly inflates the answer nearly tenfold.

**Why the emf starts at ZERO despite the loop starting "perpendicular to the field".** The phrase describes the loop's **plane**, so at \(t = 0\) the plane is perpendicular to \(\vec{B}\), which means the **normal is parallel** to \(\vec{B}\) and the flux is at its **maximum**:

\(\Phi = BA\cos\omega t\)

**A maximum of flux is a point of zero SLOPE**, and the emf is the rate of change:

\(\varepsilon = -\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt} = BA\omega\sin\omega t\)

**which is zero at \(t = 0\).** Maximum flux and maximum emf occur a quarter cycle apart — the emf peaks when the loop's plane lies **along** the field, where the flux is momentarily zero but changing fastest.

**Note the axis of rotation coincides with one arm of the loop**, and that detail changes nothing in the formula: what matters is that the loop sweeps through the field, and the flux still varies as \(BA\cos\omega t\). The axis's position affects the torque and the mechanical arrangement, not the emf.

**The rms value**, if wanted:

\(\varepsilon_{rms} = \dfrac{\varepsilon_0}{\sqrt{2}} = 8{\cdot}9\ \mathrm{mV}\)

**A sense of scale.** Thirteen millivolts from a hand-sized loop at one revolution per second is tiny — which is why a real generator uses many hundreds of turns, a much stronger field and a far higher speed. All three multiply directly into \(\varepsilon_0\).

rows.subtopic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses
rows.stem: A point source, in air, is placed at a distance of 6 cm in front of a convex spherical surface (n = \(1{\cdot}5\) and radius of curvature = 24 cm). Find the position and nature of the image formed.
rows.solution:
**Refraction at a SINGLE spherical surface**, not a lens, so the formula is

\(\dfrac{n_2}{v} - \dfrac{n_1}{u} = \dfrac{n_2 - n_1}{R}\)

**Sign convention.** Light travels left to right; the object is on the left, so \(u = -6\) cm. The surface is convex towards the incoming light, so \(R = +24\) cm. And \(n_1 = 1\) (air), \(n_2 = 1{\cdot}5\) (glass).

**Substituting:**

\(\dfrac{1{\cdot}5}{v} - \dfrac{1{\cdot}0}{-6} = \dfrac{1{\cdot}5 - 1{\cdot}0}{24}\)

\(\dfrac{1{\cdot}5}{v} + \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}5}{24} = \dfrac{1}{48}\)

\(\dfrac{1{\cdot}5}{v} = \dfrac{1}{48} - \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{1 - 8}{48} = -\dfrac{7}{48}\)

\(v = 1{\cdot}5\times\left(-\dfrac{48}{7}\right) = -\dfrac{72}{7}\)

\(\boxed{\ v = -10{\cdot}28\ \mathrm{cm} \quad\text{— the image is VIRTUAL}\ }\)

**It lies about \(10{\cdot}3\) cm from the surface, on the SAME SIDE as the object** — that is, in the air, \(10{\cdot}3\) cm in front of the surface. It is virtual, erect, and magnified.

**The negative sign is the whole of "nature".** A positive \(v\) would place the image inside the glass, where the refracted light actually travels, and it would be **real**. A negative \(v\) means the refracted rays still **diverge** after the surface, and only their backward extensions meet.

**Why it had to be virtual, without any arithmetic.** This surface's first focal length is

\(f_1 = \dfrac{n_1R}{n_2 - n_1} = \dfrac{24}{0{\cdot}5} = 48\ \mathrm{cm}\)

**and a real image requires the object to lie OUTSIDE it.** At \(6\) cm the object is far inside \(48\) cm, so the image could only be virtual — a check worth making before the substitution rather than after.

**\(6\) cm is very close indeed**, an eighth of the first focal length. The surface bends the rays towards the axis, but nowhere near enough to make them converge; it merely makes them diverge less steeply, which the eye reads as an enlarged image further away.

**Two errors this problem invites.** Using the thin-lens formula \(1/v - 1/u = 1/f\) treats two surfaces where there is one, and gives a different answer. And taking \(R = -24\) reverses the surface's curvature: **convex towards the incoming light means \(R\) is positive**, since the centre of curvature lies on the outgoing side.

**The magnification**, for completeness:

\(m = \dfrac{n_1v}{n_2u} = \dfrac{\left(1\right)\left(-10{\cdot}28\right)}{\left(1{\cdot}5\right)\left(-6\right)} = +1{\cdot}14\)

**erect and slightly enlarged** — consistent with a virtual image. *(Note this is not \(v/u\); a refracting surface with different media on its two sides carries the index ratio as well.)*

rows.stem:
(a) Differentiate between inductive reactance, capacitive reactance and impedance of an ac circuit.
(b) An ideal inductor and an ideal capacitor are connected in series across an ac voltage. Plot a graph showing variation of net reactance of the circuit with frequency of the applied ac voltage.
rows.solution:
**(a) The three quantities distinguished.**

| | **Inductive reactance \(X_L\)** | **Capacitive reactance \(X_C\)** | **Impedance \(Z\)** |
|---|---|---|---|
| What it is | opposition offered by an **inductor** to ac | opposition offered by a **capacitor** to ac | **total** opposition of the whole circuit |
| Expression | \(X_L = \omega L = 2\pi\nu L\) | \(X_C = \dfrac{1}{\omega C} = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\nu C}\) | \(Z = \sqrt{R^{2} + \left(X_L - X_C\right)^{2}}\) |
| Frequency dependence | **rises** with \(\nu\) | **falls** with \(\nu\) | depends on all three |
| At \(\nu = 0\) (dc) | zero — a plain wire | infinite — an open circuit | \(Z = R\) for dc through \(R\) alone |
| Phase | voltage **leads** current by \(90^\circ\) | current **leads** voltage by \(90^\circ\) | current lags or leads by \(\phi\), where \(\tan\phi = \dfrac{X_L - X_C}{R}\) |
| Power dissipated | **none** — energy stored and returned | **none** — energy stored and returned | only in the resistance |

**The essential distinction.** \(X_L\) and \(X_C\) are **reactances**: each belongs to a single reactive element, each introduces a \(90^\circ\) phase shift, and neither dissipates any energy over a cycle. **\(Z\) is the resultant of resistance and net reactance combined as perpendicular phasors**, and it is the quantity that fixes the current: \(I = V/Z\).

**They also act in OPPOSITION to each other.** The inductor's voltage leads while the capacitor's lags, so the two are \(180^\circ\) apart and **subtract** — which is why the net reactance is \(X_L - X_C\) and not their sum.

**(b) Net reactance against frequency for a series L-C.**

\(X = X_L - X_C = \omega L - \dfrac{1}{\omega C}\)

*To draw it:* net reactance \(X\) on the vertical axis against angular frequency \(\omega\) on the horizontal, with the origin placed so that negative values are visible.

**The shape, which is what the marks are for:**

- **At LOW frequency** \(X_C\) dominates \(\left(1/\omega C\ \text{is huge}\right)\), so \(X\) is **large and negative**, diving steeply towards \(-\infty\) as \(\omega \to 0\).
- The curve **rises**, crossing the axis at a single point.
- **At \(\omega = \omega_r\), \(X = 0\)** — mark this. Here \(X_L = X_C\), which is **RESONANCE**:

\(\omega_r = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}\)

- **At HIGH frequency** \(X_L\) dominates, so \(X\) is **large and positive**, rising without limit as \(\omega\) grows.

**Label the crossing point \(\omega = \omega_r\)** and mark the two regimes as **capacitive** \(\left(X < 0\right)\) below it and **inductive** \(\left(X > 0\right)\) above.

**What the zero crossing means physically.** With \(X_L = X_C\) the two voltages are equal in magnitude and exactly opposite in phase, so they **cancel completely** across the pair. For an ideal L-C with no resistance, \(Z = 0\) at resonance and the current would be unbounded — which is why real circuits always include some resistance, and why series resonance is called an **acceptor** circuit.

rows.stem: Differentiate between conduction current and displacement current. A capacitor is connected across a source providing time-dependent current. Explain how the total current at an instant is the sum of conduction current and displacement current in the circuit at that instant.
rows.solution:
**The two currents distinguished.**

| | **Conduction current \(I_c\)** | **Displacement current \(I_d\)** |
|---|---|---|
| Cause | actual **flow of charge carriers** through a conductor | a **time-varying electric field**, and hence changing electric flux |
| Expression | \(I_c = \dfrac{dq}{dt}\) | \(I_d = \varepsilon_0\dfrac{d\Phi_E}{dt}\) |
| Medium | needs a conductor | exists in **vacuum or a dielectric** — no charges need move |
| Charge transport | charge is genuinely carried | **no charge is transported** |
| Where it flows here | in the connecting **wires** | between the capacitor **plates** |

**The essential point: no charge crosses the gap between the plates.** Displacement current is not a current of anything; it is a **changing electric field** that produces a magnetic field exactly as a real current would. Maxwell introduced it for that reason, and the name records an old model rather than the physics.

**Why it was needed — the ambiguity in Ampere's law.**

Ampere's circuital law in its original form,

\(\oint\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{l} = \mu_0 I_c\)

**requires choosing a surface bounded by the loop, and the answer must not depend on which surface is chosen.** Take a loop encircling the wire leading to a charging capacitor:

- A **flat** surface cutting the wire is pierced by the conduction current, giving \(\mu_0I_c\).
- A **bulging** surface passing between the plates is pierced by **nothing** — no charge crosses the gap — giving zero.

**The same loop, two different answers.** The law as written is inconsistent.

**Maxwell's resolution.** He added a second term, so that the source of a magnetic field is not only the flow of charge but also the **rate of change of electric field**:

\(\oint\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{l} = \mu_0\left(I_c + I_d\right), \qquad I_d = \varepsilon_0\dfrac{d\Phi_E}{dt}\)

**Showing the total current is continuous.**

For a parallel-plate capacitor of plate area \(A\) carrying charge \(q\), the field between the plates is \(E = q/\varepsilon_0A\), so the electric flux is

\(\Phi_E = EA = \dfrac{q}{\varepsilon_0}\)

**Differentiating:**

\(I_d = \varepsilon_0\dfrac{d\Phi_E}{dt} = \varepsilon_0\cdot\dfrac{1}{\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{dq}{dt} = \dfrac{dq}{dt} = I_c\)

\(\boxed{\ I_d\ \text{between the plates} = I_c\ \text{in the wires}\ }\)

**So the TOTAL current \(I = I_c + I_d\) is the same across every cross-section of the circuit:**

- **In the wires**, outside the plates: \(I_d = 0\) and \(I = I_c\).
- **Between the plates**: \(I_c = 0\) and \(I = I_d\).

**The current never breaks.** What was a flow of charge in the wire continues as a changing electric field in the gap, of exactly the same magnitude, and the two surfaces now give the same answer.

**Why this mattered far beyond capacitors.** The added term makes a changing electric field produce a magnetic field, while Faraday's law already had a changing magnetic field producing an electric one. **The two together support a self-sustaining wave**, and solving Maxwell's completed equations gives its speed as \(1/\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0} = 3\times 10^{8}\) m/s — the speed of light. **Electromagnetic waves, and the identification of light as one, follow from this single correction.**

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.stem: What are de Broglie waves ? Show that the wavelength of the electromagnetic radiation is equal to the de Broglie wavelength of its quantum (photon).
rows.solution:
**What de Broglie waves are.**

**De Broglie waves — or MATTER waves — are the waves associated with every moving material particle.** De Broglie proposed in 1924 that the wave-particle duality already established for light must extend to matter, so that a particle of momentum \(p\) has a wavelength

\(\boxed{\ \lambda = \dfrac{h}{p} = \dfrac{h}{mv}\ }\)

**The relation contains one quantity from each picture** — the wavelength \(\lambda\) belongs to a wave, the momentum \(p\) to a particle — joined by Planck's constant. That is the whole content of duality in a single equation.

**They are not electromagnetic waves.** A de Broglie wave has no electric or magnetic field, cannot be radiated away from the particle, and does not travel at \(c\). Its physical meaning, supplied later by Born, is a **probability amplitude**: its square gives the likelihood of finding the particle at a point.

**The wavelength is inversely proportional to momentum**, which is why matter waves are invisible for ordinary objects. A cricket ball of \(0{\cdot}15\) kg at \(30\) m/s has \(\lambda \approx 1{\cdot}5\times 10^{-34}\) m — smaller than any length that has meaning. For an electron at \(100\) V, \(\lambda \approx 0{\cdot}12\) nm, comparable to atomic spacing, and diffraction becomes observable. **Davisson and Germer saw exactly that in 1927.**

**Showing the two wavelengths coincide for a photon.**

**Step 1 — the de Broglie wavelength of the photon.** Applying the relation to the quantum itself:

\(\lambda_{\text{photon}} = \dfrac{h}{p} \qquad \dots\left(\mathrm{i}\right)\)

**Step 2 — the photon's momentum.** A photon has no rest mass, so \(p = mv\) cannot be used. Its energy and momentum are related by \(E = pc\), and its energy by Planck's rule \(E = h\nu\):

\(pc = h\nu \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad p = \dfrac{h\nu}{c} \qquad \dots\left(\mathrm{ii}\right)\)

**Step 3 — substitute (ii) into (i).**

\(\lambda_{\text{photon}} = \dfrac{h}{h\nu/c} = \dfrac{c}{\nu}\)

**Step 4 — compare with the radiation's own wavelength.** For any wave, \(c = \nu\lambda\), so the electromagnetic radiation of frequency \(\nu\) has

\(\lambda_{\text{radiation}} = \dfrac{c}{\nu}\)

**The two expressions are identical:**

\(\boxed{\ \lambda_{\text{photon}} = \lambda_{\text{radiation}} = \dfrac{c}{\nu}\ }\)

**Proved.**

**Why this result is more than a tidy coincidence.** De Broglie's hypothesis was an extension **from** light **to** matter, so it had to reproduce the known behaviour of light as a special case. **This calculation is the consistency check**, and passing it is what made the extension credible: applied to a photon, the matter-wave formula returns the wavelength the photon already had.

**The two relations are the same relation read two ways.** \(p = h/\lambda\) for a photon came from \(E = pc\) and \(E = h\nu\); \(\lambda = h/p\) for matter was de Broglie's postulate. **He took an equation derived for light and asserted it for everything**, and the identity above is that assertion being tested against its own starting point.
